title: Victor Frankenstein Audits an IoT Insulin Pump
context_md:
Victor Frankenstein, Bio-Tech Security Engineer at *Geneva Labs*, is leading the security audit for a next-generation networked insulin pump before FDA submission. The device runs custom firmware on an ARM SoC, communicates over Bluetooth Low Energy with a clinician's tablet, and pulls signed firmware updates from Geneva's CI/CD pipeline.

Three concerns dominate Victor's review. First, the development team built the firmware-signing key into the build server's environment variables — Victor wants the key generation, storage, and signing operations all to happen inside dedicated tamper-resistant hardware. Second, an attacker with brief physical access to the pump should not be able to swap in a malicious firmware image; the device must verify firmware integrity before each boot, and the boot chain itself must be measured so a remote attestation server can detect tampering after the fact. Third, the company's CI/CD pipeline must catch vulnerable open-source dependencies *and* produce a machine-readable inventory that hospitals can ingest into their own vulnerability programs — particularly relevant after the Log4Shell scramble two years ago.

Victor also has to plan for the day this pump model reaches end-of-life, and he must defend against a known class of attacks where a small device is wedged between a USB port and a peripheral to silently capture data.
artifact_md:
```
Pump v2.0-rc3  pre-FDA hardware assurance review
Reviewer: V. Frankenstein   Date: 2026-05-10   Sign-off withheld.
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[FAIL]  CR-01  Firmware-signing private key stored in build-server
               env var ($PUMP_SIGN_KEY). The same OS that runs
               npm install reads the production signing key.

[FAIL]  CR-02  No per-stage signature verification at boot.
               No boot-stage measurement to platform registers.
               (Remote attestation impossible until both are fixed.)

[GAP]   CR-03  CI pipeline produces no machine-readable component
               inventory. No scanner inspects open-source
               dependencies. Post-Log4Shell guidance ignored.

[GAP]   CR-04  Source-tree static analysis: not run.
               BLE runtime test rig: not yet built (QA committed Q3).

[FAIL]  CR-05  Charging dock has exposed USB-A ports. No covers.
               No clinician warning in the ops manual.

[GAP]   CR-06  Published end-of-support date for v2: TBD.
               Hospitals cannot plan refresh budgets.
```
prompt_md: Map each `[FAIL]` / `[GAP]` line to the correct control, then click **Check answers**.
body_md:
**CR-01** is closed by moving all signing into an **{{key_hardware}}** — a dedicated, tamper-resistant device whose private keys never leave the boundary in plaintext. **CR-02** is closed by shipping each pump with a **{{platform_module}}** that stores boot-stage hashes in tamper-evident registers.

With the platform module in place, the boot process must verify the cryptographic signature on each stage before executing it: this is **{{boot_a}}**. To additionally record what was actually loaded so a remote server can later confirm the device booted clean firmware, Victor will enable **{{boot_b}}**, which extends measurements into the module's PCRs.

**CR-03** is closed by adding **{{sca_tool}}** to the pipeline to flag vulnerable open-source components, plus a **{{inventory}}** published alongside each release so hospitals can match component versions against future CVEs without reverse-engineering the firmware.

**CR-04** is closed in two halves: **{{static_test}}** against the source tree before the binary is built, and **{{dynamic_test}}** against the running firmware in the BLE rig.

**CR-06** is closed with a published **{{eol_plan}}** so hospitals know exactly when security updates will stop. **CR-05** is mitigated by warning clinicians about **{{usb_attack}}** — the class of attack where a thin malicious device is wedged in line with a legitimate USB port — and requiring port covers on the dock.

key_hardware.explanation: HSMs are network-attached or PCIe tamper-resistant key vaults purpose-built for high-volume signing operations such as a CI/CD pipeline. TPMs are bound to a single host platform — wrong scale for a build server.

platform_module.explanation: TPMs (or vTPMs in virtualized contexts) provide per-device measured-boot storage (PCRs) and attestation keys — the right primitive for an embedded device, not the build server.

boot_a.explanation: Secure Boot verifies signatures on each boot stage and refuses to execute unsigned/altered code. It is enforcement, not just measurement.

boot_b.explanation: Measured Boot records hashes of each loaded component into TPM PCRs, enabling later remote attestation. Secure Boot enforces; Measured Boot evidences.

sca_tool.explanation: SCA inventories open-source dependencies and matches them against vulnerability databases — exactly the Log4Shell-era control gap.

inventory.explanation: An SBOM is the machine-readable component inventory (formats: SPDX, CycloneDX) that downstream operators ingest to track exposure.

static_test.explanation: SAST analyzes source or bytecode without executing it — ideal for catching insecure patterns early in the pipeline.

dynamic_test.explanation: DAST exercises the running system from the outside — the right tool for finding runtime auth/authorization flaws on the BLE attack surface.

eol_plan.explanation: Documented EOL/supportability schedules are required so operators (hospitals, in this case) can plan replacements before security updates cease.

usb_attack.explanation: Shimming is the class of attack where a thin malicious device is inserted in line with a port (USB, card reader) to capture data transparently. EMI/EMP and cold-boot/rowhammer target other layers.
